Project description (required): ReleaseRoom helps software teams review an AI-generated fix together with its test evidence in one shared conversation. In a controlled support-ticket demonstration, a reviewer reports a status-filter bug in Mattermost, a genuine Codex builder reproduces and fixes it, and a separate deterministic gatekeeper independently verifies the patch. The gatekeeper hashes the diff and test evidence and exports a handoff only after the configured reviewer approves that exact current hash and the repository still matches. The recorded run uses an explicitly user-authorized approval relay, disclosed in the evidence. The output contains a review JSON bundle, a patch, and handoff notes. The public repository includes reproducible setup, protected regression tests, and the real room evidence. This is one fictional case, with no production deployment or measured time-saving claims.
How did you use Switch in your project?: We ran the official Switch 0.31.0 and Mattermost 11.9.0 stack inside Ubuntu WSL. The official agent controller bundled in Console 0.40.1 connected a genuine Codex CLI 0.166.0 builder. A custom deterministic TypeScript gatekeeper joined the same release-room through the authenticated Switch protocol. The reviewer reported CASE-001; release-builder reproduced the failing test, changed only src/tickets.ts, and posted an addressed verification request. The gatekeeper ran the protected regression test and produced a SHA-256 review hash. The user approved that exact hash in Codex and explicitly authorized the assistant to relay it through the configured reviewer account. The gatekeeper checked the authenticated sender, current hash, and repository snapshot before exporting. This relay provenance is disclosed. Switch is essential: it supplies the shared room, authenticated identities, addressing, and event transport. The gatekeeper itself makes no model calls.
What did you like about Switch, and what: The shared room and authenticated sender identities made the division between AI development, deterministic verification, and review approval explicit. The protocol allowed a small TypeScript service to participate alongside a genuine Codex builder in Mattermost. During this build, our desktop capture helper could not reliably capture the WSLg Console window, so we used the official Gateway and bundled headless controller. The first Codex test launch encountered an EPERM restriction; the agent disclosed it and retried through the normal permission flow. We would improve Windows/WSL setup guidance, version-pinned protocol examples, and connection/recovery diagnostics, with tested recipes for combining a coding agent and a deterministic service.
